subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
There is a great difference between moneys paid out by order in council and moneys appropriated by parliament in itemized form, and that is the whole point of the exception we have been taking to the large sums of money which have been paid out without being itemized. That has been the whole tenor of the criticism from the outset from this side of the house with respect to these expenditures, that they differed from all other kinds of expenditure of public moneys in that the expenditure was not itemized and as such was not subject to the control of parliament. The bill passed at the first session contained a provision that the government should be allowed to expend up to $20,000,000. That was a definite sum in a round figure. But there was no itemizing of the services on and for which that $20,000,000 was to be expended; nothing was said as to how much was to go to one province or how much to another, nothing was said as to what was to go to public works or where public works were to be carried out, nothing was said as to what was to go for other objects, either relief camps or direct relief; it was just a lump sum of $20,000,000 to be spent. Last session an amount was fixed as a maximum, but, with that exception, the different acts have simply set forth that moneys could be taken out of the consolidated revenue of the coun-r try to any amount. There was no itemizing of expenditures, no appropriations on the basis of estimates. _ I say that that was entirely wrong, and it is deceiving the public, and saying what is untrue, when a statement is made that there has been control so far as this House of Commons or this parliament is concerned over the items of expenditure in connection with relief. The truth of

the matter is that there has been no control at all. To be told what has already been spent is not to control expenditure. We have only begun to appreciate the colossal waste as a result of the indifference and lack of care and control on the part of the government over these public moneys.
Sometimes a debate of the character which we have had if it effects no other end serves to bring out declarations which otherwise might not have been made. I must say that I was gratified when I read that the Prime Minister had said on Wednesday or Thursday that he was of the opinion that the British North America Act ought to be amended and that social services in the different provinces ought to be taken over and administered by the federal government. This is what we of the Liberal party have been urging all along should be done. If hon. members will read over the discussion which took place in the house during the special session and the sessions of 1931, 1932, and 1933 they will see that with regard to unemployment relief, old age pensions, technical education and other grants in aid, I urged very strongly that there should be conferences between the dominion and the provinces with a view to bringing about financial readjustments whereby there might be turned over to the federal authority the control of social services. I urged that, with this end in view, subsidies should be readjusted in a manner that would be equitable, always adhering to the fundamental principle upon which the compromise of confederation was brought about. Hon. gentlemen laughed at the suggestion. Grants in aid to technical education was one specific case where I emphatically stated that before the government went ahead and appropriated further grants in aid, I thought that they should find out in what position the provinces and the dominion were for the carrying on of technical education, and whether it would not be better to have some of the social services, insurance against unemployment, old age pensions and the like handled as a national scheme rather than having them dealt with by the provinces in different ways, or by some of them not at all.
In connection with old age pensions we had the Prime Minister saying in 1930 that there would be a one hundred per cent expenditure on the part of the federal government-one of the numerous promises that have never been carried out. I stated that I thought the federal government ought to have the administration of the whole of that act. This was just a part of what is known as social service

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Mackenzie King
legislation. I thought that there ought to be a nation-wide scheme and national policy laid down and carried out with respect to insurance against unemployment as well as with regard to old age pensions.
The suggestion from this side has been that any relief scheme, under which millions of dollars were to be spent, should be administered by a national commission broadly representative of all parts and interests in the country; that this commission could gather information and report to parliament and thus help to lay a foundation for the changes in the British North America Act which might be necessary in order to bring about a proper national control of the great problem of unemployment, that the problem might be dealt with by national rather than provincial means.

speechtext:
They are trying to bring that about in different parts of the country by having it assumed that the province of Quebec is not going to be favourable to the amending of the British North America Act for any purpose. May I say at once to my hon. friend that I think he rose a little too soon that time; as he does very often, he let the cat out of the bag, and I do not think his speaking as he did has pleased the Prime Minister any too well. Now, however, we know the situation. The ministry opposite are desirous of having it appear -that Quebec is not favourable to an amendment to the British North America Act, and that, for that reason it will probably not be possible to get an amendment through under Liberal auspices. May I say this to my hon. friend: If he looks at to-day's paper he will find that the Conservative leader in Quebec has taken exactly the same stand as has Mr. Taschereau with respect to maintaining provincial autonomy in that province, so that so far as the question of provincial autonomy is concerned there is no doubt in the world that Quebec in that particular like every other province in Canada is properly jealous of its rights. An amendment to the British North America Act that will be injurious to their autonomy is one thing; an amendment that will serve the
interests of the provinces without prejudicing their autonomy is quite another. Where hon. gentlemen opposite make their mistake is in assuming that there will be any opposition to an amendment to the act which will help to relieve the provinces, including Quebec, of some of their burdens, and at -the same time relieve the dominion of some of its burdens by avoiding overlapping in matters of taxation, and expenditures of public moneys as is inevitable where one government raises public moneys and hands them over to other governments to spend. That obviously is not doing good to anyone but is doing injury to all.
As regards an amendment to the British North America Act wdiich would deprive the minority in any province of any right which it has, I believe that every province would be justified in opposing to the limit any such amendment. So far as this side of the house is concerned I am quite sure that any effort made in this country to deprive a minority of rights and privileges secured to it by the British North America Act would be strenuously opposed. But an amendment to the British North America Act which does not work any injury to any minority, but rather helps to relieve a majority as well as a minority of a burden it otherwise would have to bear, would be one which should very easily be brought about. If my right hon. friend had done what we suggested in this particular and appointed a national commission to administer relief and to advise him as to what legislation was necessary in order to make more effective a national scheme of unemployment insurance, old age pensions and other social services, he would not have to say what he says now, that the country will have to wait until the election is over before anything is done. He should in the existing situation have had the amendment made over two years ago. The British North America Act should have been amended in a manner that would have satisfied the provinces as well as the dominion. The fact that the Prime Minister has come to recognize that a change is necessary shows some progress, but it required a pretty strong stand and repeated urging on this side before he saw fit to make his statement. I have referred to what I said two, three and four years ago and Hansard will speak for itself in that particular. I shall read to the house what I said as recently as Monday last, a week ago to-day, and which I think caused my right hon. friend, the leader of the government, to make the statement he did on Wednesday.

As regards the endorsation by the Prime Minister of what was said from this side, may I read to the house what I said last Monday? I believe it was on Wednesday that the Prime Minister made the statement he would favour an amendment to the British North America Act which would lead to these social services being administered under a national scheme. On April 9, 1934, that is on Monday of last week, aa reported in Hansard at page 1983, it will be seen that I made the following statement :
I urged at the very first session that these grants in aid to the provinces should be stopped pending the calling of a conference between the dominion and provincial governments to see whether it was not possible to have some arrangement made whereby the dominion could assume a large number of obligations for relief in its different forms-social insurance in its various aspects-taking them over as a national obligation and in return obtaining agreements

from the provinces to amend their powers of taxation in some directions, or making concessions with respect to future subsidies. My hon. friends opposite will remember that I spoke over and over again about the inevitable consequences of continuing grants in aid at a time like this, pointing out that they meant that sooner or later the public treasury would be depleted beyond all expectation. I was hooted at by hon. gentlemen opposite for repeating this observation so often, but the force of it is coming home to them now when it is too late. I suggested then that we should seek an amendment to the British North America Act inasmuch as this question was likely to present itself with increasing urgency with time. I urged that we should at once take steps, in conference with the provinces, and by whatever course might be deemed necessary, to see whether the British North America Act could not be so amended as to give the federal government larger powers with respect to social and industrial legislation in order that we might have uniformity of laws throughout the dominion, the provinces being relieved of some obligations, having them made federal charges, and the provinces on their part foregoing, if that was equitable, their subsidies either in whole or in part.
Could any declaration be clearer than that?
I have made it in different forms during the last four years, and I made it specifically in this house on Monday last. Now the Prime Minister comes along with a statement as though the government were responsible for a policy which would lead to the British North America Act being amended in order that Canada might have a plan of national social service legislation that would serve to bring about more in the way of uniformity among the laws of the country and less in the way of expenditure of public money for the services that are being rendered. At any rate that much of good has come out of the discussion. The rest of it, so far as anything done by hon. gentlemen opposite is concerned, has been only to help to maintain this power of independence of parliament on the part of the executive, instead of seeking to have the executive continue to be as at all times it should be, responsible to the House of Commons and through the House of Commons to the people. In the circumstances I desire to conclude what I have to say by moving:
That the bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instruction that they^ have power to amend it by eliminating from it the clause which gives to the governor in council the power, when parliament is not in session to pass orders in council under the provision respecting peace, order and good government, and by eliminating from it such provisions as tend to deprive the House of Commons of its due control over the expenditure of public moneys and taxation.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to traverse at length the observations of the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King). I have only to say with respect to what I said in connection with the British North America Act I but repeated what I had said years ago, not last week, nor the week before nor the year before. While it may sooth the vanity of the right hon. gentleman to believe that his observations brought about the statement that I made, I can assure him that what I said was in reply to observations of the right hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). I merely stated what it is well known I have stated on several occasions. I think it was rather lacking in a sense of high responsibility for the right hon. gentleman to say that an effort has been made to create prejudice against the province of Quebec. The truth is that the premier of Quebec, following right after the statement that I made in this house, attacked my observations, and in the paper that I read the other evening, the Tribune, a French paper, published in Sherbrooke, the attacks were made against myself and the government because we had suggested that the act should be amended. Under the portrait of Premier Taschereau printed in that paper he was held out as being the champion, the defender, of the rights of his country, the protector of the rights of minorities, while in the statement made by myself in the house I was particularly careful to deal with that very point. I merely mention that because it does seem to me to be unworthy of one occupying the high position the hon. gentleman does, one who has been a Prime Minister of this country, to suggest that in the statement made in this house, which every member of the house heard, an effort is being made to create prejudice against the province of Quebec.
May I go a step further? The right hon. gentleman before he left office called a conference of the premiers of the provinces to discuss the amendment of the British North America Act; and a report was made, which is to be found in yonder library, and it will be found there that the result of his efforts was nothing, absolutely nil. He accomplished not a thing. That record may be read by anyone who desires to read it. The conference was abortive. And the reason was obvious.
Coming into office directly after, when the question of relief became an all-absorbing one, we discussed, as has been known to every member of this house, the question whether or not the federal government or the several provinces should be responsible for the administration of relief. And the several provinces disclaimed any intention to permit the federal power to exercise administrative privileges within their jurisdiction. And it is known in every province in Canada that while some of the provinces were not unwilling that such power should be entrusted to the federal authorities and that there should be a centralized administration of relief, there were others who as strongly insisted that it should not be so. And those others were the most powerful in point of population and wealth in the confederacy. So at that time we did not think, nor do ll now, that in a time of distress and depression it would be possible to bring about a successful conference for amendment of the British North America Act when such an attempt- failed in quiet times. I think almost every member of this house will agree that that is so. There is nothing new in the statement that the British North America Act should be amended, nor in the statement that I have said it should be amended. My saying so dates back to years before I came to this chamber. I had hoped that at the conference that the right hon. gentleman held when he occupied the position of Prime Minister he would have been able to bring about an agreement as to what the changes should be. But I say to him now, and I say to this house what every member of the house must know, that a federal commission could not function throughout this dominion unless the provinces were willing that it should, and the provinces were not and are not willing. Year after year they have stated that they desire to conduct their own relief measures in their own way, and they have done so. But the devastation wrought in Saskatchewan by nature necessitated federal relief on a very substantial scale, and other provinces were given financial aid for their own purposes and other purposes because if we helped one we should help the other. In other words their contention has been that wherever relief is necessary-and of that they are the sole judges under the constitution-it is the concern of the municipalities first, then the provinces; and the dominion, because of the magnitude of the obligations, makes grants in aid. There could be no national commission administering relief in Canada unless all the provinces were agreed. And the provinces, I repeat, have not agreed, although we were willing to undertake the responsibility. There were some provinces that were anxious that we should, but unless all were agreed, it was impossible. And the right hon. gentleman found at conferences he held in this city with the provinces to bring about

Relief Act, 1934-Air. Bennett
amendments to the British North America Act that he could not and did not succeed. Where in quiet times it was impossible to succeed I suggest that in times of great depression no one would undertake to bring a contentious matter such as that into the realm of discussion with respect to matters of relief.
Secondly, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) is reported to have said that all the expenditures were laid on the table of this house and that the details have always been available to the right hon. gentleman.

That is what I used to say to the right hon. gentleman about the Montreal harbour bridge. It is passing strange how interested he becomes in these academic applications of principles when he is out of power. It is passing strange how he neglects them when he is in office. It is passing strange that he should talk about a blank cheque to-day when he took from parliament a blank cheque under which more than $19,000,000 was spent, without anything being indicated as to how large the amount was to be when he took the cheque. Why this sudden conversion? Have we converted him by what we have done and said so that he realizes the necessity now of relying upon parliamentary control in dealing with these matters? I could name many other instances which occurred when he was in office; there is nothing new about this method. Whenever he wanted to do it in connection with railways he did so. What about the three steamships built on the Pacific coast, the three steamers about which the Minister of Railways said he did not know the money was to be spent for that purpose? What about the order in council for the hotel that was to be built in Vancouver, in connection with which the expenditure has amounted to twice the sum contemplated by the order in council, which was cancelled? What about these things? "Consistency, thou art a jewel." When I hear, in that perfervid oratory of the right hon. gentleman, talk about the departure from principles and the injury done to the body politic, and how future generations will rise up with these precedents to the great danger of democracy
I ask who, for nine years, taught democracy the lesson? Look at that harbour bridge in Montreal. When the Minister of Finance delivers his budget address he will show that one of the reasons for putting a tax upon the Canadian people was to find half a million dollars for that bridge, after giving credit for the amounts received from the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal. Was there any talk then about Durell? Were there any observations then about Redlich? Were any statements made then about the necessity of putting in the measure the sum of money to be spent? And what is more there never has been the audit that was provided for in this case.
These are facts to which I direct attention; that was fact No. 2, and now I proceed to deal with fact No. 3. It is said that the blank cheque is detrimental to the interests of the country as a whole. The other evening I explained that any statement in a bill that a minimum sum of money is available is but an invitation to the provinces to see to it that the whole of that sum is expended. I did not expect then to receive approval from such a high source as the former Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), who stated that this was the most powerful argument that could be made against stating a specific sum, and that he wholly agreed, that this was his view also. Most thoughtful men believe this is so. So far as peace, order and good government is concerned, I merely point out in regard to this matter that it has been discussed and re-discussed and that everything has been said about it that could be said. The right hon. gentleman has been even reading his own speeches to this house lest we forget what was said on previous occasions. This afternoon we heard him read the speech he made on Monday last, only a week ago. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) read three of these speeches by the right hon. gentleman the other night, so altogether it seems to me that Hansard will well preserve all that might be usefully said with respect to this matter.
Now I should like to say a word with respect to the audit. The right hon. gentleman has said that the auditor general made certain test audits, on the strength of which he wrote letters. I say, as I said in the house the other evening, that the facts do not warrant the allegations made by that gentleman; I say that frankly. Here is the document upon which the Minister of Labour was supposed to act, in part; it is the report of the Department of Labour on direct relief expenditures in the province of Ontario.

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Bennett
Exhibit A is the report to the Minister of Finance dated December 27, 1933, and signed by Georges Gonthier, auditor general. I find here a report to the auditor general from Edmund E. Stockton, dated August 15, 1933. Mr. Stockton was named by the auditor general as his representative to make the investigation in Ontario. Mr. Stockton made the investigation; he made his report on August 15, 1933, and so little did the auditor general regard the irregularities that he sent it to the Minister of Finance on the 27th day of December, 1933. That was the nervous anxiety he felt for the body politic in the expenditure of public money; the report was not transmitted to the Minister of Finance until December 27. Subject to the above observations I am of the opinion that in the municipalities visited the inspection and audit by provincial inspectors is sufficient to safeguard the interests of the federal treasury.
Those were his words. Then, the last paragraph :
I desire to express my appreciation of the courtesy extended to me by the various provincial and municipal officials and others whom I interviewed during my visits to the offices mentioned in this report.
Respectfully submitted,
Edmund E. Stockton.
He goes on to describe the methods which have been adopted, and to show what was being done by the inspectors to ascertain whether or not expenditures were in proper form. That was the summary he made.
Now, I put this to the House of Commons again:	The auditors of the provinces in my
judgment are men of reputation and of honour, and I have no reason to believe that the municipal authorities are other than men of honour. The provinces being responsible 
for the expenditures, in the sense of having undertaken by agreement to supply us with certificates signed by provincial auditors and by the provinces themselves, I still believe that the federal exchequer was properly protected. And if it had not been, as I indicated the other evening, the provinces must refund us the money. The auditor general's letters have been very sweeping in their statements, and he will have to endeavour to justify them before the public accounts committee. If they are not different from what I have seen he will have great difficulty in doing it. That is the other side of the question. Why have we had delays in receiving accounts from the province of Quebec? Why did we not receive any accounts from July until only the other morning? Why? Because the province of Quebec has an auditor who was not willing to certify accounts until he was satisfied they were correct. He has not certified accounts which he did not believe were correct. That was the reason for the delay,-because he had to satisfy himself. He knew he was pledging himself, his reputation and his name to this particular matter. There is the story. All I can say is this, that to assert there has been negligence requires greater proof than I, at least, have seen evidence of. If there is one thing in the world I have endeavoured to be particularly careful about, it has been the administration of the finances of this country. When I say that in every instance a certificate was prepared we provided that there should be a certificate by the auditor of the province, and signed by the province, I believed that we had taken all the steps which were necessary. It may well be that there may be some deception here and there. I suppose it is within the memory of hon. members in this house that even in the Dominion of Canada auditors have been deceived extending over a period of years, and that the offender was at last found out. There is no promise of infallibility either in connection with the man who spends money or the man who checks the expenditure of money. All one can do is to ascertain the extent to which sound business rules have prevailed. Where there were expenditures made by the municipalities and certified to by the provincial auditor, that the total expenditure was x and the share of the dominion was y, and where we paid y because of the certificate given by the auditor of the provinoe, it would be difficult to say that in that step there was any fraud or negligence, or a disregard of ordinary business rules. It may well be, as shown in connection with the prosecutions carried on in the province of Ontario, and one or two other provinces, that there were individuals who

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Bennett
endeavoured deliberately to defraud the country. But the fraud was on the municipalities and the provinces, and when the provinces found it out they took the necessary steps to expose it. So far as our accounts are concerned adjustments immediately followed, because we are in the happy position of being able to retain moneys which by investigation it is found have been improperly paid to the provinces, it being remembered that the cheque of the dominion goes to the provinces and not to the municipalities. Therefore, as between the provinces and ourselves, any difficulty of that kind can. be overcome.
There is another matter to which I was rather surprised the right hon. gentleman referred. He read from section 7 of the bill now before the house, and if he had taken the trouble to look at the interpretation act he would have found that the section in this measure is that found in all such statutes. It merely provides that anything which has been done by regulation, before it has been repealed shall not be vitiated by reason of the repeal. It is a standing rule of interpretation in our statutes. The section is as follows:
All orders and regulations of the governor in council made hereunder shall have the force of law and may be varied, extended or revoked by any subsequent order or regulation; but if any order or regulation is varied, extended or revoked, neither the previous operation thereof nor anything duly done thereunder shall be affected thereby, nor shall any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred thereunder be affected by any such variation, extention or revocation.
It is true that the right hon. gentleman is not a member of the legal profession, but he has had a wide experience, and he graduated in law. He knows well, or should know, that that provision is found in the revised statutes of our country, and is a rule in interpretation which has statutory force and effect. It has to be included in all matters of this kind. Wherever a statute provides that regulations shall be made under its provisions, this clause is inserted to protect those who act under the regulation before it has been either amended, revoked or altered. That is all there is to it.
But, much as was my surprise that the right hon. gentleman should make such observations as he did with respect to section 7, I confess I cannot understand why he should have suggested to this House of Commons the possibility that under the provision for peace, order and good government we could extend the lifetime of parliament. Who knows better than he does that that is in the British North America Act; who knows better than he does that that is an imperial statute; who
knows better than he does that a delegated power conferred upon an executive can never be higher than the power granted to the parliament which confers it. As this parliament itself could not extend its lifetime, except under the provisions set forth in the British North America Act, it did seem to me to be playing rather small politics to suggest to the people of Canada that under the provision for peace, order and good government this government could extend the lifetime of parliament. I think that careful-shall I say thoughtful-people who read that statement will place a great discount on everything which the right hon. gentleman has said. For it cannot be suggested that anything is added by way of argument when one suggests something which every hon. member in this house knows cannot be done by this parliament itself, much less by the executive, under a delegated power.
Then the other suggestion was that we had taken the power to disallow provincial legislation, under the grant of power to legislate for peace, order and good government. There again it must be obvious to even the most thoughtless member-if there are any, and I trust there are not-that it would not be possible for us to exercise any such power.

I said it was suggested; I did not say the suggestion was made by the right hon. gentleman. The power of disallowance is in the British North America Act itself, and that statute stands until it is amended by the power which created or enacted it. We cannot amend it; we cannot alter it, we cannot repeal it. The power that is^ there conferred is a power that this legislation does not touch, nor does this legislation touch any power which is in the constitution to be exercised by the parliament at Westminster, nor does it touch any powers that are conferred by the constitution exclusively upon the legislatures. What it does is, within narrower limits than those suggested by some hon. gentlemen, to confer upon the executive the power to make regulations for the peace, order and good government of the country under conditions in which it may seem necessary to the executive to exercise such power. But those powers as defined by the privy council are much less broad than some hon. gentlemen have suggested. I cannot in the very nature of things make a legal argument to this house showing that the limitations imposed upon the words are far greater than would occur to the ordinary individual not trained in the inter-

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Bennett
pretation of the constitution. If hon. gentlemen are interested they will find that they are the opening words of section 91 of the British North America Act itself so far as the power is concerned, and the enumeration of the powers in section 91 is an enumeration of powers that does not limit the generality of the terms of the general power conferred. The jurisdiction conferred upon the executive by this parliament under peace, order and good government is, as I have said, under the decisions of the privy council a rather restricted jurisdiction. But it is sufficient to serve our purposes in the event of any untoward circumstances requiring the exercise of such power.
The other matters that were referred to I think have been sufficiently dealt with in what has already been said in other years with respect to this legislation. I repeat, this legislation is not sought for any purpose other than the public good. I repeat, parliament is being asked to confer authority upon the executive peradventure it might be required. If necessary it is there.
I am not going to follow the example of the right hon. gentleman and discuss the marketing bill which stands for second reading to-day. But this I will say, that in all the legislation that was passed during the nine years the right hon. gentleman was in office, wherever it became essential or necessary to clothe the executive with power to make either regulations or rules or to do any acts that might be essential for the well-being of the country, that power will be found conferred upon the executive. No hon. member can tell me that there is any difference between conferring an unlimited power upon a harbour commission to guarantee bonds for the construction of a bridge and the conferring of power by the parliament of Canada upon the executive to take necessary action to provide relief for Canadians who are in necessitous circumstances. The principle is the same. Then why not frankly admit it and say: The principle is the same but we think that this power may peradventure be abused.
I said the other evening, and I say now, that no hon. gentleman can point to a single abuse of that power nor to any usurpation of authority nor to any deprivation of rights nor to any effort, successful or unsuccessful, on the part of the executive to do any act or thing except for the good of this dominion- not one; and I repeat that, in order that there may be no misapprehension with respect to the matter.
I have spoken at greater length than I anticipated but when one realizes the unreal-

ity of a discussion such as this, realizes that all these things that are now being condemned were once being done by the right hon. gentleman who now condemns them and that he would have to do them again to-morrow if he were similarly situated, that all these high heroics and histrionic efforts are, shall I say, but a passing phase of the work of an opposition that regards it as its sole duty at all times to oppose, when it is suggested that because of something said in this house last week this government or myself have learned something-I am always learning something, Mr. Speaker, and I trust that I always shall as long as I live-but with no desire to cast aspersions on the right hon. gentleman at all, I say to him that I have not learned anything from him with respect to matters of this kind. I say that without intending offence. When he suggests that because of something he said in the house last week I have changed my mind, the chances are that because he said it my mind would be more likely to remain just where it was. He should not betray his anger and annoyance because there are others who have as advanced thoughts as himself-

Mr. Speaker, I have had very little to say with respect to the measure now before the house. I do not desire to detain the house on the third reading of this bill but I should like in a word to make the position of some of us clear with regard to our votes upon it.
This is a case in which one might perhaps almost be justified in giving either an affirmative or a negative vote. We are anxious to

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Woodsworth
have a very large measure of relief, the largest measure of relief possible, and for that reason we might very well welcome a bill of this character.
Further, I have not been tremendously impressed by some of the arguments advanced by the official opposition. I do not desire to discuss to-day the question of democracy. In my judgment democracy does not necessarily mean that every measure must be submitted to parliament or to the people. Democracy in my opinion is not at all inconsistent with prompt and efficient action on the part of the executive. But I have to oppose this bill because I believe it is hopelessly inadequate as a relief measure. After all these years, when the government have had full opportunity of working out some constructive scheme, we are still simply being asked to acquiesce in the general idea that the administration is going to do something about the situation. When the measure was first introduced I pointed out that we had had no definite intimation as to what the government proposed to do with regard to a program of public works. I think we ought to have had that at the very beginning of this session. No hint of it is contained in this measure.
Further, we have had before us for many years the promise that there would be some kind of unemployment insurance scheme during the lifetime of this administration. There is nothing whatever contained in this measure with regard to that.
We have had this present government denouncing the dole and yet itself resorting to one of the worst forms of the dole that I have ever heard of, a dole that is absolutely insufficient to provide for the needs of large numbers of Canadian families in this country. I receive daily the most pathetic letters asking that something should be done to help to prevent the breaking up of homes and to give adequate food to the children of the citizens of this country. I do not consider that the measure now before us provides that kind of thing and because I feel it is inadequate, I cannot vote in favour of it.
I object to having these wide powers for peace, order and good government interjected into a relief measure. If we were facing a great emergency it might be necessary for the government to assert certain of the powers which it has under the British North America Act, but I protest once more against a government taking powers of this kind under a relief measure. For these reasons, some of us will have to vote against the bill although we are most heartily in favour of a relief measure.

A special meeting of town council was held Tuesday to decide what action would be taken to help fishermen obtain gear. After considerable discussion, a resolution was passed that the federal government be asked to establish a fund of not less than $15,000 under the proposed marketing and credit legislation, through a system of loans for purchase and equipment of boats. Copies of the telegrams were sent to Hon. E. N. Rhodes, Minister of Finance; William Duff, M.P. for Antigonish-Guysborough and William A. Found, Deputy Minister of Fisheries.
In addition to my receiving the telegram which I read to the committee, according to this dispatch the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), who is the minister from Nova Scotia, received a similar telegram as did the deputy minister of fisheries. No doubt that latter gentleman passed on the telegram he received to his minister, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau). speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was verj'' much interested this afternoon in listening to the definition given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) of the constitutional rights of the dominion and the provinces. I was interested also in the answers which the Prime Minister gave on Friday evening to a question put by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury). It should not be forgotten that the dominion is the creation of the provinces. There never would 'have been a dominion government and we would not be now sitting in this house if the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, New Bruns-
wick and Nova Scotia had not agreed upon our creation. The powers which we exercise here were exercised formerly by the provincial governments-our powers are delegated powers. Quebec has been mentioned and I would say that the rights of that province are common to all provinces.
The greatest fights since confederation have been carried on by the English-speaking provinces. The warrior bold and the great champion of provincial rights was Sir Oliver Mowat who downed Sir John A. Macdonald in connection with many bills with regard to provincial rights. Who forgets the great fight earned on by Manitoba with regard to its educational rights? Who forgets the great fight carried on by New Brunswick on that same question? It is strange, but it happens that in this country the greatest fights we have had have been on the educational question. The population of Canada is composed mainly of two of the leading races of the world. Without Quebec there never would have been a confederation because Quebec, being situated in the middle, immedately between the maritime provinces and Ontario, consented to confederation, and in doing so gave up many rights. When Quebec consented to confederation it was in full possession of its powers, but it abrogated many of them in the hope and with the promise made to Sir George Etienne Cartier, Sir Etienne Paschal Tache, leaders of the Conservative party in power at that time, to Antoine Aime Dorion, to the Fourniers and the others, that not only the letter but the spirit of the law would be respected. I am proud to be able to say that to-day it is the boast of my province that it has carried out that undertaking of confederation not only to the letter but in the spirit also. If anybody wishes to be informed on that point, let him go to Quebec and inquire of the English-speaking citizens of that province; let him inquire of the Council of Public Instruction, the Protestant section, how the educational law is being carried out there and he will find in Quebec a breadth of view which I hope will some day prevail in every province.
Let us remember that we are Canadians. We are all proud of the country from which we sprang. Those who came from French stock have nothing to be ashamed1 of nor have those of British extraction. While we have had in this country men from all races, the French Canadian has played his part, not only in establishing this dominion but in its constitutional development; in the parliamentary field no man has ever surpassed those who have been produced by the French Canadian

Relief Act, 1934-Air. Marcil
people. Of course Quebec was then a minority; it is a minority still and when questions arise as to amending bargains, constitutions, contracts, because the terms of confederation after all constitute a contract, it is only fair and reasonable that the people who will be primarily affected do not want to consent to any radical changes without knowing what they mean. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) say to-day that this is not the time, when the country is in the position it is, to undertake to bring about those changes in a haphazard fashion or merely for the purpose of bringing them about. If you want to do anything in this or any parliament, the legislation which you may introduce must be backed by public opinion. If we had had the same cooperation at the beginning of the war as we bad later we would have avoided many unfortunate happenings. War was thrust upon us by Germany; we did not seek it. I was not elected in 1911 to go to war with Germany; I had no mandate from my constituents to send one, two, three or half a dozen contingents overseas, but we had no choice; we were at war. Canada was a British possession and had Britain been defeated, the German warships'could have ascended the St. Lawrence and laid in destruction every town and village in our province. We had to face the ordeal as it existed.
Canada, like all other countries, especially like all confederations, will survive only if there is mutual give and take. If we want our rights respected we must respect those of others and I am glad to know the feeling of the leaders of the two great parties in this house and even of the third leader, because the leader of the C.C.F. has spoken along the same lines, in regard to tinkering with the constitution. The constitution has been amended on several occasions, and I have been in the house when amendments have been made. That was done by consent. Many amendments to the British North America Act are to be found in the statutes, but they were probably agreed to by the dominion and the provinces themselves; there was no trouble about that. The people of any ^province, when a matter is brought to their attention and it is shown to be necessary in the public interest, will consent to an amendment. The constitution, of course, is not the laws of the Medes and Persians; it can be amended, but it can be amended only with the consent of the provinces because it was made with their consent, and under the rules of any game, no contract can be changed without the consent of the parties interested.

I am an old timer. When I came into parliament in 1900, we could not vote a dollar without its being placed in the estimates, passed through committee of supply and committee of ways and means and put down in black and white. I have heard debates here last for days and days in regard to very small amounts, a question of principle being involved. In the past parliament has abrogated its rights and we are abrogating them again to-day. The Prime Minister has said that no attempt has been made to go beyond the terms of the power that he has; that in what he desires to do there has been no abuse contemplated. But the principle is there. By the measure we are passing to-day we are putting into the hands of the cabinet, a committee of parliament, power to do anything they like to do under the sovereign for the peace, order and good government of 'Canada. That covers the whole field. In other words, it is a repetition of the War Measures Act. That act, which I opposed in the house and which was strongly opposed by the Liberal party generally, gave to the government of the' country full power of awarding contracts without tenders and, in fact, of doing anything under the sun. Under this clause the same power is being taken to-day and that is the main objection I have to the measure. We are all in favour of relief; we have all said so and we say so again, but something which should be sacred in every parliament is that the authority which raises taxation should have control over the spending of the money. We are abrogating that right. A great deal of federal money has been spent in my constituency; we have to vote for it but it is expended by the provincial government. The people of my constituency elected me to represent them in the federal parliament, but we simply raise the money here, send it to another government to spend and then, when the spending has been done, we are called upon to vote for an expenditure about which we know nothing.
This is on a par with the administration of our railways. We were told only a few days ago that the committee that looks into the estimates of the Canadian National Railways would be called. I have asked in parliament many questions that as a representative of the people I have to ask as to how this money and that has been spent and how much has been spent in my constituency. This question concerns fundamental principles of government. I have been, however, refused an answer because I am told that it is not in the public interest. We have taken the creatures, the servants of this house, this parliament, and

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Marcil
we have placed them above us, whether it be the chairman of the international joint commission, or of the railway commission, or of the pension commission, or of the civil service commission, or of any of the, I was going to say, one hundred and one commissions that we have created, because we now have government in Canada by order in council and by commissions. We have abrogated our rights, and that is contrary to the very essence of parliamentary government. The principles involved would take too long to state and explain now, nor is this the time to do so. I merely want to register another protest against departing from a principle which has been sacred in the history of the British constitution. It was asserted in England for generations and for centuries that there should be no taxation without representation. The people's representatives secured control of the public purse, and at the close of every parliament the last words that come from the representative of the king are the assent which he gives to the supply bill. Now we are abandoning that control. Those who come after us may blame us for that, but we are doing so voluntarily, except those of us who protest, of whom I am one.
Not only are we going to advance money to the provinces, which of course is a way of giving to the provinces money that we should spend ourselves, but the government are taking power to grant money by way of loans, guarantees or otherwise, to the Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited. Then why should they not do so for the fishermen's associations and for the various associations of farmers in the eastern provinces? It may be said: Well, wheat is the great product of the country; millions of dollars worth are produced by the western people. As the Prime Minister said the other day, there is no country in the world in which so much wealth has been raised by so few people, in so short a time as that from the head of the great lakes to the foot of the Rockies, the great wheat fields of Canada. During all my time in parliament I have been prepared to support all measures for the benefit of the west. Let us never forget that it was the Liberal party and its policies which placed a million people in that western country. I had the honour many years ago when I was deputy speaker of this house of attaching my signature to the bills creating the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. So the Liberal party did what it could for the west in those days. To-day it is being blamed in many speeches for building too many railways. There was a time when every member from western Canada was predicting that one transcontinental railway was not enough, that

two were necessary and that the time would come when half a dozen would not be too many to carry the output of that great prairie country. The west is but beginning after all. How much is under cultivation at the present time? Not more than fifteen or twenty per cent of the land that could be made productive. But that is another question.
I want to refer to the wants of my own people. As I said on Friday, I have received over a hundred petitions from all parts of the province of Quebec, signed by farmers, in favour of the fisheries of the Gaspe peninsula and of Quebec. I want to read just one of these petitions so that it will be on record and in the hope that when the Prime Minister comes to afford the relief he intends to afford under this bill he will not forget the settlers in this country, whose ancestors came to Canada many years ago, and who are now in deep need; men who have not been favoured with the bountiful crops raised in the west, who do not possess such fertile lands, but who nevertheless have stood by and done their share for the upbuilding of Canada. I should like to see the government do what it can under these relief measures to bring about a better understanding between the dominion government and the provincial government regarding this moot question of the fisheries of Quebec, as to which at present there is conflict. In view of the appointment by the Prime Minister of the committee on price spreads this question should be inquired into in the maritime provinces as well as in Quebec. I think it my duty to read this petition.

This is not a petition
addressed to parliament, it is rather in the shape of a resolution adopted by these people. I want to read it so that the government may be apprised of the situation in which these people find themselves.
(Translation):
Maritime fisheries of the Province of Quebec*
Whereas the maritime fisheries of the province of Quebec, located on the St. Lawrence river, the Gulf and Bay des Chaleurs, interest a population of at least 100,000 souls partly depending on the fisheries for a livelihood.
Whereas, since 1922, the government of the province of Quebec have taken over the fisheries on the high sea.
Whereas it is difficult for the Quebec government, without aid, to give the service supplied by Ottawa, in connection with maritime fish-

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Motherwell
cries, because such service already exists with its program, experts, scientific institutions, coastguard vessels, assistance to fishermen and many other facilities which are impossible for the Quebec government to undertake side by side with that established by the Dominion government.	.
Whereas the federal service extends to the other provinces where fishing on the high sea is carried on, moreover, this service, so highly organized, is partly defrayed by the taxes paid by Quebec and from which the latter receives no benefit.	. .
Whereas the organization of the maritime fisheries on a more profitable basis for the fishermen of the province of Quebec, the theoretical and practical instruction, the establishment of purchasing and marketing co-operative associations can be better undertaken through the medium of the dominion authorities. _
Consequently the people of the province of Quebec who depend on our martime fisheries are at a market disadvantage compared with other fishermen of British Columbia and the three maritime provinces.
Therefore, it is moved by....
Seconded by....
And resolved:	_	_
That the associations of "l'Union catholique des cultivateurs" on behalf of their members, request the cooperation of the dominion and provincial governments to improve the lot of the maritime fishermen of the province of Quebec.
We respectfully insist that there should be some arrangement between the said governments this year, and we further request if it is necessary, the repeal of the 1922 order in council transferring the exclusive control of the maritime fisheries of Quebec to the provincial government.
We make this request from a purely human, economic and national viewpoint.
We, therefore, beg of the Minister and members, both federal and provincial, to examine this question on its merits, so that both governments may come to an agreement in this connection.
Briefly they ask that there should be cooperation between the federal and the provincial governments in coming to the relief of the fishermen of Quebec who are now in a very, very difficult position. I hope the government will give effect to this view and bring about an understanding by conciliatory methods with the province of Quebec. Quebec at the present time is administering its inland fisheries, but in the maritime part of the province the fisheries were left under the control of the dominion, the Magdalen islands for instance. Naturally the inland fisheries are a matter for the provincial government, but the maritime fisheries should be, I believe, administered jointly by agreement with the province. The Minister of Fisheries for Quebec says, as reported in a Quebec paper two or three days ago, that he had made several attempts to bring about an understanding with the dominion government. I am not familiar with all the negotiations that have taken place, but he claims that so far he has been unable to succeed.
I bring this matter to the attention of the Prime Minister hoping that, in accordance with what he said a short time ago, he will be able to afford relief in cooperation with the provincial government. He cannot do so otherwise because it is a matter of provincial concern with which we would have nothing to do unless these terms relating to peace, order and good government were in the measure. I hope the Prime Minister will give my remarks full consideration and try to bring about an understanding with the government of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, any goverment that has had one of its major measures so consistently and strenuously opposed by the opposition as has been the case with this relief bill should not be surprised if we register our last protest on the motion for third reading before the bill passes and goes to the other chamber. That is the usual practice in all similar cases. If the government believe the country is on the way to recovery surely they should be getting away from this class of legislation instead of reverting to it, as they are doing now. Either the government does not believe its own ballyhoo with regard to recovery or it is enacting this legislation, which is more severe than the legislation last year, for some other purpose, and the nearness of an election suggests that that has something to do with it. One of my colleagues was sufficiently good natured to absolve the government from any suspicion of that kind, but I know what this government are capable of doing. Judging from the redistribution bill of last year, which was corrected in two or three particulars in a way as to which I have expressed my appreciation, but which nevertheless was a drastic gerrymander, I say that any government that will take that action will take advantage of this legislation.
There are many ways in which they can do so. We do not forget the wartime election, when certain overseas votes were bunched where they would do the most good. What about the public works program? Can it not be bunched where it will do the most good? If the government are given a free hand and an unnamed amount of money with which to do nearly as they like between now and next session, who can say what may happen? If it is a fact-and it has not been denied- that under this legislation this government can precipitate Canada into a war without calling parliament together, then I am emphatically opposed to it. I do not want to talk about war unnecessarily; I remember the injunction given us some time ago not to

Reliej Act, 1934-Mr. Motherwell
talk about war too much. 1 quite agree, but I can recall the last war, to which the country was committed to the hilt before parliament met. I for one do not want that to occur again, and if this can be done under this legislation-and I believe it can-that alone is sufficient reason for me to make my last protest against it, which I do with all the vigour of which I am capable.
Then there is another point, of which I have spoken at least twice, but the more I think of it the more audacious the conduct of the government seems to have been. I refer to these guarantees in connection with the sale of wheat on the Winnipeg market by Mr. McFarland. Just think of taking the credit of Canada, to an unknown amount, and putting it behind a wheat market stabilization policy with not a report to parliament even once as to the amount involved for three and a half years. I have no doubt the government was well enough intentioned in this matter, but we have had the people's money and the people's credit used continuously for more than three consecutive years, with no accounting to the owners of that credit or the owners of the wheat. The government may have accounted to the pool authorities through Mr. McFarland but they have not accounted to the individual contract signers who owned that wheat, or to parliament. So I repeat that this government, which preaches business ethics to others, is in danger of becoming a castaway itself. They preach nobler ethics for chain stores and mail order houses, but do as they like with unnamed sums of money which they can spend at any time, anywhere, any how. This is done under the direction of one individual, and I do not care how white he is; the whiter he is the worse it is, because he is put in an invidious position in which no straight man would want to be placed, and I do not believe Mr. McFarland wants to be put in that position either. Unquestionably he has the guarantee of this country behind an aggregate credit amounting to at least 8160,000,000. That is our guess; we cannot find out the exact amount, so we have to guess at it. Give anybody, with the knowledge of the market that Mr. McFarland unquestionably possesses, control of practically the whole hedging operations of not only the pool but the entire grain trade and he can do as he likes with the option market in regard to jigging it up or down to the advantage of this or the other class of people. I doubt if any hon. member will challenge that statement. Mr. McFarland has almost entire control of the hedging operations of that market. Has he power to throw it in favour of or 
against any particular class of the community? If he has that power it is no use telling me that he will not use it; if the power is there it is an extremely dangerous power, and I strenuously object to it.
I suppose these words will be interpreted by some as casting some discredit or doubt upon the honour of Mr. McFarland. I am not doing anything of the kind. I happened to have the opportunity at one time of seeing the marvellous vaults of a great insurance company in Montreal. These vaults, with their ponderous electrically operated doors, contained bonds and securities to vast amounts, deposited by many governments and municipalities, corporations, and so forth. I was told that no one, whether an employee or not, ever was given access to those vaults alone. Was that a reflection on the individual, because someone else was sent with him when it was necessary to look into any of those deposits? No, that was a safeguard, and every honourable man in that great insurance company would rather have someone accompany him than have access alone to all those securities. On that occasion I asked a gentleman who was with me how he felt about it, whether he felt that it was a reflection on his honour to have someone accompany him when he went to the vaults. He answered, "No, it is my desire that I should be accompanied; then I will not have to take the whole responsibility alone." So it is with Mr. McFarland. I take the ground, as I think Mr. McFarland would, that he would much rather operate on that market with two or three -associates, especially when he is operating with a government guarantee and a continuous account. I do not see why, for the time being, the government could not make Mr. McFarland a member of the board of grain commissioners, which has the confidence of western Canadians to an exceptional and peculiar degree. I think the people there also have enough confidence in Mr. McFarland to believe that if he were added to the board it would make for the better administration of that line of credit. So there would be more confidence throughout the country than is the case when those operations are handled by one man, even though he be the best that ever stood in shoe leather. We do not forget that Winnipeg was recently the home of a man in whom great confidence was reposed, but who failed his friends and his trust. This shows the danger of unnecessarily placing implicit confidence in any one individual. For these reasons I think the government has done itself a great injustice in defiantly refusing to give this house any information with regard to this wheat guarantee. I give the

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
government this last opportunity, which apparently they are not going to take, to tell them that so far as I am concerned the government is the worst friend Mr. McFarland has, although the right hon. Prime Minister is supposed to be the millionaire chum of Mr. McFarland, another millionaire. That will not make the temper of the people any better at this time. I must again avail myself of the opportunity to speak upon this point, although I wish I had been deprived of that opportunity by a candid statement by the Prime Minister.
I have been predisposed to look upon Mr. McFarland as an honourable man. But just as it is not fair to give such a trust, alone, to the men in the insurance companies to whom I have referred, who have charge of the vaults and are undoubtedly honourable, so in this instance it is not fair to give such great responsibility to Mr. McFarland alone.
I could go on further and make observations regarding some other guarantees. However the right hon. Prime Minister has said that he does not believe any special power which has been granted to this government has been abused. I cite this particular instance as one in which it has been abused-unnecessarily abused-and the people have been audaciously flouted by being refused information in connection with their own business.

Mr. Speaker, I believe this bill is worthy of some comment, before the house proceeds to third reading. This is one of the most important measures which will come before parliament this session, and the passing of similar legislation is becoming an annual affair. Hon. members interested have in my view a perfect right to express their opinions upon the provisions of the measure now before them. It is quite true that with all the vigour we possess we have opposed the passage of some sections of the bill. We have taken the same action at each session of parliament in which we have considered similar legislation. Further, if we are to have another session of this parliament we will be forced to give further opposition, because I cannot conceive of a complete cure so long as the policies of the present government are in effect.
Without generalizing too much may I state that the government secured its present position by very spacious promises made to the electors. They did not promise to relieve unemployment; they promised to cure it. And not only did they make that promise to the electors in 1930, but they made other promises. They stated that unemployment had reached a stage where it had become a
national question, one which was too great for the provinces or municipalities to handle, and which should be assumed by the federal government. If there is anything in conmeiction with which this government have changed their policy, it is unemployment and unemployment relief. I can recall their statements made on the platforms in 1930 that they were going to end unemployment and take it over as a national obligation. During the special session of 1930 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) introduced his bill he told us that it was a measure to provide work and wages. After a term the government decided that the giving of work to provide wages was too expensive and they changed their policy to one of -direct relief. Apparently they have got tired of direct relief and are going to put on a program of public works. In- the short space of four years the government have turned right-about-face several times in connection with unemployment and unemployment relief.
During the course of -his remarks to-day the Prime Minister said that I had agreed with him on Friday evening, and he seemed to take some comfort out of that fact. Either he did not understand What I said or he twisted

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Heenan
my argument around. My argument was in accordance with the one advanced by the right hon. leader of this party (Mr. Mackenzie King), that whatever money this parliament spends should be spent under its own control. My remarks appear in Hansard of Friday, and here is what I said:
To-night the Prime Minister advanced the best argument that I have heard as to why the act should be amended.
I was referring to the British North America Act.
The right hon. gentleman said that if we state a definite amount in this bill the provinces will clamour for what they think is coming to them; even if they need only $2,000,000 if there is $20,000,000 to be divided they will want their share. I think the Prime Minister was right in that argument; I agree with him, and that is just another reason why we in this federal parliament should take care to see to it, when we are spending money, that rve spend our orvn money over which we have control.
If the Prime Minister can get any consolation out of those statements, I am glad to let him have it. The argument I advanced is that which has been advanced continually by the opposition, that when we are spending money we should spend our own money and should take control over it. If the government had carried out their promises to the elecwiv. they would have taken control and assumed the obligation of unemployment and unemployment relief. The government told the people in 1930 that they would make it a national obligation and they received a mandate from the people to take over unemployment and unemployment relief as a national obligation. Will anyone contend that the government of Quebec or of any other province would object to this government taking over full control of and assuming full reponsi-bility for unemployment relief? I am certain that no government would object. The fact that we have this bill before us in 1934, four years after this government was elected to end unemployment, is the best proof that the policies of this government have failed. A policy that has been put into effect by this government and that has lost trade to the extent of SI,768,000,000 in four years, must have been a poor policy and one not in the best interests of Canada.. Surely the policies of a government that has lost trade to that extent in four years, that has added four hundred million to the debt of this country and that has increased taxation until the people are overburdened with it, cannot be good for this dominion. Therefore I repeat that this government has from time to time changed its ideas and its policies, and the worst feature of the matter is that it has not
carried out its direct promise that if it did not do these things it would perish in the attempt.
I do not need to repeat that those who need relief, those who are working under relief measures, are getting by all odds the small end of the deal, and this government, not content with bringing in a measure of this kind for unemployment relief and having it administered by the province of Ontario in the way it has been, have coupled with it the peace, order and good government provision and all those other matters that have no connection with an unemployment relief measure. I agree entirely with the leader of the C.C.F. party in asking: Why include in the relief measure the peace, order and good government provision and ask for additional powers to maintain peace and order in this country over and above what already exists on the statute books. I contend that while the government are handing out relief with one hand, in the other we have a bludgeon that if the people do not like the relief, then they must be quite subservient and take what is handed to them by the Conservative government or suffer the consequences.
Then this government takes power-and I would not mind if it lived up in some way to the powers that we give it-to make regulations. In connection with the fact that I stated a moment ago that the labour men got the small end of these things, I want to point out that the Minister of Labour-and of course that means the government-has changed his position in regard to the wages that are to be paid to men engaged on these works. If we take the report of the dominion director of unemployment for 1930, there will be found on page 15 regulation No. 7 which reads as follows in connection with the wages that are to be paid:
7.	All agreements made with provincial or municipal authorities involving the expenditure of any portion of the moneys appropriated by the act for public works or undertakings shall contain provisions for the payment of fair wages and hours of work in accordance with the intent of the Fair Wages and Eight-Hour Day Act, 1930, and the fair wages policy of the government of Canada as set forth in order in council (P.C. 1206) dated 7th June, 1922, and amendments thereto.
That is what is known as a minimum wage, a fair wage, but at any rate it works out as a minimum wage. According to the report of the dominion director of unemployment relief for 1932, that policy is entirely changed, because we find among the general regulations clause 8 on page 3 as follows:
The federal government will require that a maximum work day of eight hours shall prevail on works and undertakings carried' on under the provisions of the Unemployment

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Heenan
and Farm Relief Act, 1931, unless a modification of this requirement is previously agreed to by the minister; the provincial or municipal authorities may fix rates of wages to be paid provided that such rates be fair and reasonable and not in excess of the rates required to be paid by the federal government for the character or class of work in the district.
In other words, the first regulation that was put there by the dominion government on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour was a minimum rate of wages and when they changed their policy in the following year, as shown in the 1932 report, they had a maximum rate of wages. For the information of hon. members who may not be acquainted with the minimum and maximum rate of wages principle, when an employer is limited to a minimum rate of wages he cannot pay below that, but when there is a maximum wage set, he does not need to go to the maximum, but he can pay as low below it as he sees fit. In other words, it is a destruction of the minimum rate of wages. Here we have a government telling the labour men of this country what they have done for them in the face of the intelligent electors, barefacedly including in their regulations a provision that neither the provincial nor the municipal authorities can pay more than the federal government do for works of a similar character. Had the Minister of Labour and the government required them to pay as much as the federal government did, I would not mind that, because I am sure the minister, so far as federal works are concerned, will have a minimum rate of forty or forty-five cents an hour for labour men in his own riding and, in fact, throughout most of northern Ontario. Yet he allows the provincial government in the case of works for which money is contributed by this government to pay $5 and $10 a month.
